https://www.dw.com/en/us-envoys-meet-wit.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Le7B US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were back in Moscow for more talks with President Vladimir Putin Image: Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday evening. "The situation is of course not simple," Putin told the US officials in footage aired on Russian state media. Putin and US envoys held "useful" talks on a range of ideas to end the war in Ukraine, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters. According to Russian media outlets, US envoys left Moscow after the meeting. Earlier, US President Donald Trump said Kushner and Witkoff were traveling to Russia with a new proposal, but he did not provide any details on the potential peace plan, including whether it involved Ukraine giving territory to Russia as he has previously suggested. Instead, he said, "We have an idea for peace." In the meeting with Putin, Kushner and Witkoff discussed "substantive plans" for the next steps toward ending the Ukraine war, the White House said, adding that more details would be announced next week. The envoys "look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine," a White House official said in a statement. Russia, Ukraine pause strikes for three days The Kremlin said Russian forces would pause strikes against Kyiv for three days in conjunction with the peace negotiations. Putin "ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told state media. The order came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had already committed to pausing airstrikes for the talks. "As with previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are concerned about their safety, not about Russia," Zelenskyy said. US envoys to make first visit to Kyiv Zelenskyy announced on Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would visit Ukraine on Sunday following talks in Moscow. Recent media reports have questioned whether the pair would indeed travel to Ukraine. Despite trips to Moscow to meet with Russian officials, the US envoys have not visited Kyiv since Trump's reelection last year. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he had been in contact with Kushner and Witkoff. "I ⁠have ​just spoken ​with the US president’s ​envoys," Zelenskyy said ‌on Telegram. "From the moment of this conversation, ​we ⁠are ready to observe a ⁠ceasefire ​in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process." Trump had promised to end the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, on his first day back in office, but has more recently said that the feat was more complicated than expected. In the past, he has blamed Ukraine for the Russian invasion and a "personality problem" between the countries' leaders for the continued fighting. https://www.nation.sc/articles/32216/un-.text: Domestic UN tells the world: Stop making Africa look small |08 September 2026 Robert Dussey, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Togo (at podium and on screens), introduces the “Correct the map” draft resolution (UN Photo) UN tells the world: Stop making Africa look small The United Nations General Assembly has overwhelmingly endorsed a resolution encouraging the use of world maps that more accurately show the relative size of continents. The resolution, supported by 164 votes to one, was backed by an African-led campaign challenging the continued dominance of the 16th-century Mercator projection. The United States was the only country to vote against, while Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained. https://voiceofvienna.org/latvias-pro-eu.text: RIGA: Latvia’s pro-European Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs has won a commanding victory in the country’s parliamentary election, securing a mandate to continue his government’s firm support for the European Union and Ukraine, according to Hurriyet Daily News. Kulbergs’ centre-right United List won 42 of the 100 seats in parliament, an unprecedented result in Latvia’s post-independence political history. The outcome gives him a strong position from which to begin coalition talks, although he will need new partners after one party in his previous alliance failed to cross the five per cent threshold needed to enter parliament. The election was fought against the backdrop of anxiety over neighbouring Russia, rising living costs and wider social concerns. While Kulbergs’ party dominated the result, populist movements also made gains, drawing support in part from Latvia’s Russian-speaking minority. Speaking after exit polls pointed to his party’s sweeping success, Kulbergs said the result exceeded his expectations. “That means people truly want change,” he said, describing that change as economic growth and a secure future for Latvia’s children. Kulbergs, a former manager in the telecommunications and automotive industries, became prime minister in May at the head of a centre-right coalition. His victory now allows him to pursue the pro-European and pro-Ukrainian policies that have defined his government. The election also revealed a strong current of populist sentiment. Latvia First, a conservative party led by a property magnate often compared to US President Donald Trump, finished second with 17 seats. The right-wing Sovereign Power party was on course for third place with 15 seats after campaigning heavily on the cost of living. Sovereign Power has opposed military aid to Ukraine and further increases in defence spending, positions that place it at odds with the governing mainstream. Its strong showing underlines the political tensions in a country that shares a border with Russia and remains highly alert to regional security threats. For Kulbergs, the task now is to translate an exceptional electoral result into a stable coalition. His success suggests that many Latvian voters want continuity in foreign policy, even as economic pressures and populist appeals reshape the country’s political landscape. The document, filed in Washington federal ⁠court, charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information.
